reasons: Etymology sound: ON bíta < PGmc *bītan- < *bʰeyd- = Skt bhid-, Lat. findo (Kroonen s.v. *bītan-); hjarta ~ hṛdaya (*ḱerd-). But the collocation is not congruent. In Þormóðr's verse (context: a leech follows) the iron 'bit' with heart as a locative goal, hiarta (dative) governed by næsta 'nearest', not 'split the heart'. In MBh 3.255.28 bhinna- in a bahuvrīhi compound with hṛdaya ('with split heart') after an arrow in the chest. ON bíta is the ordinary unmarked verb for any weapon cutting, so its use here is not a lexical choice that could carry a formula. Once the drift to 'bite' is admitted, all the two passages share is 'a weapon wounds the heart', which any warrior literature produces (bíta+hjarta co-occur only once or twice in the Norse index). Latin finditur (of cor) is emotional, not a weapon wound.

The cognates are good: Arm. tam / Gk δίδωμι / Skt dā (*deh₃-) and Arm. dowstr / θυγάτηρ / duhitṛ (*dʰugh₂tḗr; Martirosyan s.v. dustr), with kin < *gʷen-. Both Armenian anchors have 'give' + 'daughter' (+ 'as wife'): Movses has zdowstr, iwr, tay, kin + dative, and in Faustos the king says he wished to give 'you my daughter' as wife (possessive im, not reflexive iwr). Thucydides 6.59.3 has θυγατέρα, ἑαυτοῦ, ἔδωκεν + dative. Still, 'father gives his daughter (as wife) to X' is the default way of expressing a patrilocal marriage, and both words are the basic inherited terms, so their co-occurrence is expected (dowstr+tam co-occur in 17 of 99 dowstr units). The Armenian knowtʻiwn / kin also matches biblical Greek γυναῖκα (with εἰς), which raises a translation or calque risk for 5th-century Armenian prose. Neither Norse anchor shows the phrase in its passage line: AM-35 146 is about naming a son (jós, gaf, nafn), and AM-35 228 names Tosti's daughter (het, dottir). The gipta wording is only in the context lines and uses a different verb (gipta, a renewal), so it adds nothing. Defensible as an inherited collocation, but not distinctive.

reasons: Both roots are exact cognates: bera / φέρω / bhṛ (*bʰer-) and nafn / ὄνομα / nāman (*h₁nómn̥). The Norse passages read as claimed: AM-35 228 has bæri + nafn with tígnar, and in AM-178 Samson refuses the kongsnafn (nafnn + bera). Herodotus 1.32.9, however, uses the middle φέρεσθαι 'to carry off, win (as a prize)' with οὔνομα. That is the prize idiom, not 'bear a name', so the Greek collocation is only loosely congruent. 'Bear a name/title' is a cross-linguistically trivial metaphor: Lat. ferre/gerere with nomen, German tragen with Namen, English 'bear'. The roots co-occur often (25 Norse and 160 Greek units in the index). The Norse witnesses are medieval prose. AM-178 is the Samson/Salerni narrative of Þiðreks saga, which was transmitted from continental sources, so a learned or calqued origin is possible. The Vedic support, nā́ma with bíbhrat, is the best evidence, but it is not an anchor.

The passages read as claimed: Hesiod Op. 563 has γῆ with μήτηρ (nominative, in apposition), and AVŚ 18.3 (the funeral verse also found in RV 10.18.10) has mātaraṃ with bhūmim, object of sarpa. Only one element is cognate, μήτηρ = mātṛ (*méh₂tēr). The Earth nouns are not cognate (γῆ against bhūmi/pṛthivī), and the claim concedes this. 'Earth as mother' is one of the most widespread personifications and arises independently, which is a generic risk. The contexts also differ (agricultural yield against burial). Plausible as an inherited figure, given Vedic mātā with pṛthivī beside pitā with dyauḥ, but the anchors share no wording beyond 'mother'.

The etymology holds. Kroonen derives ON garðr / Go. gards < *gʰordʰ-o- and explicitly compares Skt gṛhá- < *gʰr̥dʰ-ó-, and EWAia s.v. gṛhá- compares Go. gards. The kin terms are exact cognates in the genitive. The Norse text has dotter, leghen, faður, garðe, moðor, broðor (AM-302) and faður, garðe, broðor (AM-56 w926/w929), on the inheritance share of a daughter seduced while in her guardians' homestead. AVŚ 1.14.4 has mātuḥ, badhyatām, gṛhe, bhrātuḥ, pituḥ, a spell binding a girl to stay unmarried, as Yama's bride, in her natal house. Against this: 'in the father's house' is a generic phrase in any patrilocal society, and the triad of guardians follows from the social facts. Order and coordination differ (eða against atha), and the legal context (inheritance penalty) is unlike the AV curse. The Norse is a 13th-century Christian law code. The anchor AM-56 w854 is about the giftingarmaðr and has no house-word, so it does not support the claim. The best feature is the cognate house-noun with the kin genitives, which is not enough to pass the generic bar.
